title: Section 136 — Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

enhancement.definition: BNS s. 136 provides that whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both, subject to the same Explanations as Section 131.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Mitigates the penal liability for minor physical threats or non-injurious force when provoked by immediate grave and sudden indignities that deprive the actor of self-control.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 136 (corresponding to IPC s. 358).
Actus reus: Assaulting (s. 130) or using criminal force (s. 129).
Mitigating condition: Committed on grave and sudden provocation given by that person.
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to one month, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both (fine modernized from ₹200 under IPC 358).
Explanation: Explicitly incorporates the Explanations to Section 131 (the three provisos restricting provocation and declaring provocation a question of fact).
essentialIngredients: The accused assaulted or used criminal force against the victim.
The act was done on grave and sudden provocation given by the victim.
The provocation deprived the accused of the power of self-control.
The provocation was not sought as an excuse, done in obedience to law, or in lawful private defence.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 136 carries forward Section 358 of the IPC. It serves as the provocation counterpart to Section 131. Where an individual is provoked by grave and sudden insult or conduct, loses self-control, and responds with an assault (e.g., brandishing a hand) or simple criminal force (e.g., shoving the provoker) without causing bodily hurt, Section 136 applies. The punishment is mitigated to a maximum of one month imprisonment, a fine up to ₹1,000, or both. The section is governed by the same statutory provisos as Section 131: the accused cannot claim provocation if they deliberately invited it, if it was given by a public servant acting lawfully, or if it was given in lawful private defence.
examples: Teaching example (Provoked shove): A person is abruptly subjected to a filthy, unprovoked verbal obscenity directly regarding his family by an antagonist; enraged and deprived of self-control, he immediately shoves the antagonist backwards without causing pain or injury. This falls under s. 136 (up to one month or ₹1,000 fine).

Teaching example (Disqualifying proviso): A police officer lawfully stops a motorist at a checkpoint; the motorist claims the stop is a 'provocation' and brandishes a fist at the officer. Under the Explanation, acts done in obedience to law cannot constitute provocation; s. 136 is unavailable and s. 132 applies.
distinctions: Section 136 vs Section 131: Section 131 applies to unprovoked assault/force (up to 3 months); Section 136 mitigates the punishment to 1 month due to grave and sudden provocation.
Section 136 vs Section 122(1): Section 136 applies when assault/force is used WITHOUT causing hurt; Section 122(1) applies when the provoked act causes actual hurt.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who raised a walking stick threateningly at a person who had just spit on his shoes can claim mitigation under s. 136.
Rule: Assaulting a person under the immediate influence of grave and sudden provocation given by that person is punishable under BNS s. 136.
Application: Spitting on someone is an extreme indignity constituting grave and sudden provocation; the retaliatory gesture was immediate.
Conclusion: The accused is entitled to mitigation under BNS s. 136.
